Abstract 
Purpose: To investigate technical regulation mechanisms of long-distance swimmers that 
differentiate optimal pacing strategies and the underlying kinematic parameters. 
Methods: Twenty-one national and international swimmers equipped with a sacrum-worn 
IMU performed during 5000m indoor French championships. Percentage of critical swimming 
speed (CSS), stroke rate (SR), stroke length (SL), jerk cost (JC), stroke index (SI), and 
mechanical proficiency score (MPS) were computed by lap. Athletes were divided into groups 
of pacing effectiveness based on optimal potential performance level (OPPL) -optimal 
(nearOPPL) and suboptimal (farOPPL)- using functional clustering of %CSS. Race sections 
were analyzed with a change-in-slope detection method. Common stroke regulation abilities 
and deviations by pacing groups were profiled by fitting hierarchical generalized additive 
models between mechanical variables and laps. 
Results: The two clusters were discriminated by %CSS sustainment (p<0.01). Optimal 
performers showed a +41.4% more stable pacing (2 race sections vs. 3 for farOPPL) and a 
+36.7% higher end-spurt, with a trend combining higher overall SR (p=0.08) with lower JC 
(p=0.17). Functional profiles showed that maintaining a higher SL and SI in a fatigued state, 
rather than overall values, allows to reach OPPL (p<0.001). High regulation of MPS across the 
race, in line with pacing expectations of particular race sections, is a game-changer to sustain 
CSS (p<0.001). 
Conclusions: Specific profiles of stroke regulations, regarding tradeoff between stroke 
smoothness and resultant speed, lead to optimal pacing during 5000m. The results of this study 
enhances the technical understanding of an optimal pacing in long-distance pool races for 
coaches and swimmers. 
Keywords: swimming, race strategy, critical velocity, kinematics, open-water

Introduction 
Pacing strategy is crucial for achieving successful competitive outcomes while maintaining a 
tolerable physiological state, as it involves managing homeostatic disturbances through a 
balance between energy availability, fatigue but also technique.1 Properly regulating exercise 
intensity can therefore lead to optimal performance.2 The optimality of pacing strategy in 
endurance events, such as long-distance swimming, can be individually evaluated based on an 
athlete's capabilities concerning critical swimming speed (CSS). The latter is associated with 
the highest sustainable metabolic rate (E)3, explaining the upper limit of sustainable aerobic 
power.1 
Accordingly, recent evidence suggested that critical speed (CS) is at least as explanatory of 
endurance performance level and pacing strategy as maximal oxygen consumption (𝑉′𝑂2𝑚𝑎𝑥), 
lactate/ventilatory threshold, and energy cost (C) of locomotion.1 Therefore, considering the 
individual regulation of CSS during long-distance swimming may provide new valuable 
insights into better pacing strategies. Previous research in other activities has shown that world 
records in 10km running, for example, are performed close to CS.4 Thus, an athlete's ability to 
maintain an average speed as close as possible to his individual CS, through finely-tuned 
pacing, may define his optimal potential performance level (OPPL). Nevertheless, despite the 
identification of this performance determinant in successful pacing strategies for endurance 
events, there remains a crucial lack of information in long-distance swimming. Specifically, 
the control of individual CSS supporting OPPL, and more importantly, the understanding of 
the underlying biomechanics, have not yet been investigated. 
Appropriate pacing is especially critical in swimming due to its low mechanical efficiency.5 
Therefore, durability or physiological resilience, becomes critical in long-distance swimming, 
and has not yet been studied, whereas it should be considered an additional component in 
models of endurance performance and optimal pacing.6 However, it remains unclear whether 
kinematic changes are dependent on durability features.7 Achieving OPPL, i.e. sustaining the 
highest possible fraction of CSS, seems highly dependent on swimming technical abilities, 
which regulate stroke mechanics over the race. For instance, a previous study showed that 
theoretically optimal pacing, from an energy flow model, had negative technical consequences 
and did not result in better performance in 1500m speed skating.8 Despite the increasing 
amount of research on swimming pacing to determine whether there is an absolute optimal 
performance template9, there is still a scarcity of data analyzing pacing strategies in long-
distance swimming during real competition settings.10,11,12 This effect becomes even more 
evident when examining individual swimmer capacities (i.e., CSS) and the underlying 
regulation of stroke mechanics. Notably, many federations have now integrated long-distance 
pool events (e.g., 3000m and 5000m) into their regular competition schedules, mainly because 
fast open-water swimming requires higher speed in middle- and long-distance pool 
competitions.13 Accordingly, it offers elite open-water swimmers an effective means to 
enhance their speed and refine specific pacing strategies.10 Consequently, the lack of data limits 
the understanding of performance determinants in these events, hindering the ability to achieve 
individual OPPL and effectively design training plans for both long-distance and open-water

swimmers. A previous study on elite 5000m pool races revealed that top performers typically 
use an even pacing strategy.10 However, the study did not examine the underlying kinematic 
factors related with this strategy. The authors showed that medalists tend to have a non-
significant lower average stroke rate (SR) than non-medalists. Similarly, in world open-water 
events, no significant differences in overall SR were observed between successful and less 
successful swimmers. Instead, the ability to vary SR throughout the race was more closely 
related to the final performance level.14 Indeed, while it is well established that the ability to 
maintain a given swimming velocity based on SR or stroke length (SL) has a direct and positive 
impact on performance, the continuous regulation of technical aspects underpinning pacing 
remains unclear. Consequently, only speculations about the biomechanical mechanisms at play 
can be made.15 
However, few studies reported kinematic data associated with pacing regarding performance 
groups. It leads to no clear evidence about speed management profiles with respect to stroke 
mechanics patterns and performance levels of swimmers.16 Only11 provided lap-by-lap 
kinematic data over a 3000m pool race, but independently of final performance. The authors 
showed that fatigue negatively affected swimming kinematics (i.e., SL and stroke index (SI) 
were reduced while SR increased between the two halves of the race), but they did not provide 
the underlying biomechanical mechanisms, allowing for recommendations about the regulation 
of pacing and associated swimming technique, to reach individual OPPL. Apart from SR, SL, 
and SI, jerk cost (JC) also reflects substantial technical abilities. JC quantifies movement 
smoothness, a universal indicator of skilled and efficient movement17. Thus, JC has been 
recently applied to evaluate technique18, discriminate biomechanical abilities19, and profile 
stroke regulations leading to success in open-water.20 Therefore, JC may provide valuable 
kinematic insights to understand the requirements to achieve OPPL pacing and tailoring the 
development of associated specific technical skills. 
The present study aimed at identifying technical regulation mechanisms through patterns of 
kinematics that maximize the maintenance of CSS to distinguish optimal pacing strategies 
during a 5km indoor national championship. 
Materials and methods 
Subjects 
The study included 21 national (tier 3) or elite level (tier 4)21 swimmers (11 women, age: 
18.0±4.17 y.o.; World Aquatics points in long-course 1500m freestyle: 606±68.9 and 10 men, 
age: 17.5±1.78 y.o.; World Aquatics points in long-course 1500m freestyle: 661±65.8). All 
participants signed an informed consent form in agreement with the French Ethical Committee 
(approval 2021-A00250-41). 
Design 
Each swimmer competed during the 2023 French national championship of indoor 5km. The 
race density was 13.5%, 10.3%, 5.61%, and 6.73% for each heat, respectively, with an overall

This speed to jerk cost ratio reflects the magnitude of stroke smoothness degradation necessary 
to achieve the swimming speed, serving as an overall indicator of mechanical swimming 
proficiency. 
The swimming speed for each lap was expressed as a percentage of the CSS (%CSS). CSS 
values were determined as the slope of the distance-time relationship derived from swimmer’s 
best performances in long-course 400m, 800m, and 1500m.25 This individual speed 
standardization enabled the assessment of performance effectiveness (i.e. optimality). 
Therefore, an average speed of 100 %CSS over the 5000m was considered the individual 
OPPL. 
Statistical analysis 
Statistical analyses were conducted using RStudio (Version 4.2.2, RStudio, Inc., Boston, MA, 
USA). The level of significance was set at p<0.05.  
Functional clustering of performance 
To profile the effectiveness of speed management (i.e., proximity to the OPPL), we employed 
the funFEM method to cluster time series of %CSS. This functional data analysis framework 
enables the clustering of times series based on a discriminative functional mixture model.26 
Visualization involved computing mean cluster curves to assess pacing effectiveness. Clusters 
were ranked as (sub)optimal performance based on their proximity to the OPPL, and technical 
explanations of pacing behaviors were provided accordingly. To do so, data were presented by 
cluster as mean±standard deviation per 200m and averaged over the entire 5000m. Pairwise 
comparisons using t-test and Bonferroni correction were used to investigate the link between 
cluster with the overall relative swimming performance (i.e., %CSS) and the calculated CSS, 
as well as the mean kinematics (i.e., SR, SL, JC) across the 5000m. The magnitude of 
differences was interpreted by effect size using Cohen’s d with threshold values of 0.20, 0.50 
and 0.80 defining trivial, small, medium and large effects, respectively.   
Race section data-driven analysis 
To identify race sections within each cluster of pacing effectiveness, we used the slope change 
detection algorithm developed by Fearnhead et al.,27 The identified changepoints defined 
specific race sections over the 5000m for each cluster, representing distinct periods of pacing 
regulation, which were analyzed regarding inferred slope and interpreted as the effect of race 
section laps on %CSS. 
Technical regulations supporting pacing effectiveness 
Hierarchical Generalized Additive Model (HGAM) was employed to evaluate and compare the 
underlying technical regulations across the 5000m within each pacing cluster. The HGAM 
allows to model nonlinear functional relationships between the laps and kinematical variables 
(SR, SL, JC, SI, MPS) as well as intergroup variability.28 This approach illustrates how 
kinematics evolve continuously for all swimmers, as well as how it varies between groups (i.e.,

Results 
Pacing effectiveness profiling 
Mean cluster curves describing the functional regulation of %CSS by laps are presented in 
Figure 1. The best model identified two clusters of %CSS management that showed no 
dependence on sex ( χ²(21)=0.02, p=0.88). These distinct patterns of control define pacing 
effectiveness and are particularly differentiated by the ability to maintain significantly higher 
average %CSS over the 5000m (p<0.001, d=1.94, Table 1). Consequently, the clusters were 
named the nearOPPL and the farOPPL class and, interestingly, there was no significant 
differences in CSS between them with 1.46±0.07m/s and 1.44±.09m/s respectively (t(13.9)=-
0.43, p=0.67, d=0.19). Additionally, Table 1 indicates that there is no significant difference in 
averaged kinematics between the two clusters of potential performance. However, there is a 
tendency for swimmers in the nearOPPL cluster to have a higher SR (p=0.08, d=0.80) and a 
lower JC (p=0.17, d=0.61).

Segmentation in pacing according to cluster  
Three and two distinctive sections of %CSS management across the 5000m were respectively 
identified for the farOPPL and the nearOPPL clusters. These specific windows were 
correspondingly determined by 2 changepoints at lap 45 and 90 for the farOPPL class, and 1 
changepoint at lap 90 for the nearOPPL class (Figure 2). They were interpreted as two main 
race parts defining pacing control, with a global section from start to lap 90 (divided into two 
subsections for the farOPPL cluster around lap 45) and a common end-spurt section from lap 
90. The associated model parameters were presented for each race part in Table 2. It described, 
for the swimmers belonging to the farOPPL cluster, an overall 41.4% higher lap effect on 
%CSS decrement during the global section (i.e., 115.5% higher lap effect decrement from lap 
1 to 45, despite a 42.0% lower lap effect decrease from lap 45 to 90) and a 36.7% lower lap 
effect on the end-spurt section.

Discussion 
This study aimed at identifying discriminative patterns in technical regulations that maximize 
CSS sustainment. For this purpose, we defined 100%CSS as the maximal theoretical swimming

speed sustainable at physiological steady-state.1,3 Our main findings highlighted the underlying 
biomechanical mechanisms of pacing during a national 5000m indoor competition, indicating 
that specific profiles of stroke abilities lead to OPPL. This work enhances the kinematical 
understanding of achieving an optimal pacing on an individual level and supports the 
development of associated distinctive technical skills. 
Pacing and global kinematical characteristics of the optimal performers 
The swimmers of the nearOPPL cluster demonstrate a better ability to sustain %CSS 
throughout the race. It seems not associated with absolute CSS value as such nearOPPL 
swimmers display a non-significant difference of +1.37%. Since CS approximates the 
physiological intensity of the maximal lactate steady state and the second ventilatory or lactate 
threshold29, these swimmers are closer to their OPPL and can be defined as optimal performers. 
Additionally, such pacing characteristics may reflect better physiological resilience, as 
indicated by their higher durability in maintaining individual CSS.6 While durability is likely 
crucial for explaining endurance performance, the mechanistic basis of this physiological 
resilience remains unresolved6, particularly in swimming. Further research is needed to 
integrate biomechanical regulations and changes in technique that contribute to optimal pacing 
and then performance.15 
Pacing analysis over the 5000m allowed us to identify performance features. Notably, the best 
profile of pacing effectiveness demonstrated fewer race sections compared to the farOPPL 
cluster, with 2 segments versus 3 segments, respectively. This greater variability in intensity 
across the race among farOPPL swimmers is a possible characteristic of lower-expertise 
swimmers, who may more deviate from their planned strategy due to the influence of other 
swimmers.9 In contrast, the optimal performers exhibited the ability to maintain a more stable 
pacing pattern in terms of %CSS decrement throughout the global section. Indeed, reducing 
pacing variability, excluding the first and last laps of the race, helps save energy and has been 
associated with better performance on 1500m compared to a fast-start strategy30, confirming 
the optimality of the nearOPPL cluster. However, we did not observe such a mitigated fast-
start for those swimmers. This may indicate that in longer pool races such as the 5000m, 
swimmers may perform a fast start without detrimental consequences on pacing and final 
performance as traditionally found in 400m, 800m and 1500m.15,9 It could be explained by 
starting a 5000m pool event with an above average swimming speed while apparent 
homeostasis for blood lactate, blood glucose, 𝑉′𝑂2, E and C.12 
Additionally, the magnitude of %CSS management is also largely distinctive. Optimal 
performers showed a better preservation of %CSS at 41.4% until lap 90. It corresponds to end-
spurt launching, detected for both clusters at the same point, but with a higher extent of 36.7% 
for the nearOPPL cluster. The ability to trigger a dramatic increase in swimming speed is a 
distinguishing feature of performance in both pool and open-water swimming.31,32 
Furthermore, the magnitude of this decisive end-spurt largely depends on the pacing strategy30 
but also to the anaerobic reserve and the speed in shorter races (i.e., faster pure swimming 
velocity).13 Indeed, a more preserved anaerobic capacity accounts for additional nonoxidative 
energy during exercise above critical intensity (D’).33 Consequently, optimal performers could

preserve a higher D’ through precise intensity balancing and/or enhanced work capacity above 
CSS, enabling a more effective end-spurt34. Finally, monitoring both %CSS management and 
D’ as key requirements for success, could deepen the understanding of optimal performance in 
long-distance swimming. 
However, one can wonder about the technical adaptations that support such optimal pacing. 
Interestingly, the aforementioned distinctions between the two clusters were not accompanied 
by significant differences in averaged kinematics. Nevertheless, a trend was observed where 
the nearOPPL swimmers exhibited a 5.43% higher SR and a 23.7% lower JC, with large and 
medium effect sizes, respectively. The higher average SR of the better performers aligns with 
previous data on pool events35 but seems discordant with open-water swimming 14, where 
regulating SR throughout the race appears more important.20 This may explain the better %CSS 
maintenance of the nearOPPL cluster during the global section of the 5000m. More 
importantly, the reduced overall JC of the nearOPPL cluster is crucial for understanding the 
technical requirements of optimal pacing. High JC leads to explosive technique, typical of 
sprints19 or impaired technique in long-distance20, which increase E.36 Consequently, such a 
stroke pattern might be unsustainable over 5000m, ultimately impairing performance and 
taking away from OPPL. Indeed, nearOPPL swimmers’ higher stroke smoothness indicates 
better technical skills, consistently with top rankings during international open-water events 
regardless of their CSS-related performance optimality.20 Finally, such improved smoothness 
at higher SR may reflect discriminative technical skills that could explain achieving OPPL 
pacing.  
Technical regulations of the optimal performers  
Both SL and SI controls turn to be a crucial underlying kinematical regulation supporting 
optimal pacing. Each of them follows a global positive profile that highlights a continuous 
decrease that can be attributed to fatigue-induced impairment in applying effective force in the 
water37, reflecting a decline in arm action effectiveness. These reduced decrements for the 
optimal performers may explain their success. Indeed, SL is traditionally regarded as the single 
best predictor of swimming performance. SI essentially describes the ability to maintain a given 
velocity with the fewest number of strokes, indirectly reflecting technical efficiency in 
converting strokes into forward propulsion and swimming economy, since high SI is strongly 
associated with low E.24 However, this specific feature of the nearOPPL swimmers contrasts 
with previous literature suggesting that SL maintenance could negatively affect 1500m elite 
performance.35 Moreover, the ability to maintain a higher SL in a fatigued state, rather than 
overall SL -since nearOPPL swimmers has a 1.55% smaller average SL than farOPPL 
swimmers-, appears to be a distinguishing feature to achieve optimal pacing during long-
distance swimming. These findings echo recent evidence from marathon running, which 
highlights that athletes with greater durability tend to preserve “fresh” biomechanical 
parameters than those with lower durability.7 
Finally, the management of MPS follows a common parabolic-shape with a downward 
opening, reflecting the requirements of the conservative pacing conducive to OPPL. Therefore,

farOPPL swimmers exhibited a logical deviation attenuating the shared MPS pattern that 
indicates non-regulated mechanical proficiency. 
Until lap 50, maximizing MPS involves reducing the speed-to-jerk cost ratio by a smooth motor 
pattern at race pace implying less intra-cyclic kinematical variability. Such a technique might 
minimize C and may indicate improved mechanical efficiency.5 Thus, swimmers adopt specific 
kinematics to maximize the conversion of acceleration variations into speed with an 
economical technique. Such behavior aligns with the requirements of middle- and long-
distance swimming, as well as open-water events, which demand high stroke efficiency.20 
Subsequently, our MPS tracks this expectation through the ratio between actual speed 
production and associated stroke smoothness, representing an insightful easy-to-monitor 
variable of technical effectiveness and performance. Further investigations are nevertheless 
required to more deeply understand the physiological implications of MPS maximization. 
After lap 50, the MPS progressively decreased due to a mismatch between degradation of 
stroke smoothness and the resulting swimming speed. A higher JC might lead to faster 
swimming with adequate technical skill.18 Thus, targeting a decay in stroke smoothness, 
leading to improved acceleration fluctuations, suggests applying more force in water to sustain 
CSS, despite decreased stroke efficiency, as evidenced by the drop in MPS. This technical 
adaptation aims to achieve effective parabolic or even strategy, as previously demonstrated in 
3000m and 5000m.10,11 Thus, nearOPPL swimmers align their mechanical efficiency in light 
of pacing expectation, defined by specific race sections, as shown by high MPS variations. 
Reduced MPS, due to a jerky technique, possibly indicate higher E36, with optimal performers 
having higher energy supply to sustain such C. However, the physiological expectations for 
achieving such biomechanical regulation and pacing to sustain CSS in long-distance swimming 
remain unclear. Therefore, further in-situ assessments considering the interactions between 
physiological profiles, durability, and technical skill regulation is crucial for maximizing 
performance7, and offer an exciting approach to better understand technical explanatory factors 
of durability and optimal pacing in long-distance swimming. 
Practical Applications 
Technical explanations leading to OPPL in long-distance swimming have been benchmarked 
as the combination of high overall SR with stroke smoothness. The underlying regulations of 
stroke kinematics throughout the race seems fundamental. Firstly, maintaining SL in a fatigued 
state, rather than the overall value, is distinguishing to achieve OPPL. Secondly, optimal 
performers highly regulate their MPS across the race, by aligning it with the specific 
requirements of race segments, to lower C or maximize acceleration variations. This is 
achieved by continuously balancing the trade-off between stroke smoothness degradation and 
the resultant speed. The present study can assist coaches and athletes in designing training 
sessions targeting the ability to effectively manage stroke smoothness according to pacing 
demands. This might be achieved using various technical constraints (e.g., adjusting the 
expected number of arm strokes per pool length), at different intensities and after diverse 
distance swum.

Conclusion 
The present study highlights discriminant race features for maximizing CSS sustainment in 
long-distance swimming leading to better durability. The approach used, combining both 
pacing and technical profiling, enabled innovative race analysis with embedded sensors. Our 
findings emphasize the importance of both stable pacing and a high-magnitude end-spurt, but 
more importantly, the underlying technical regulations to achieve individual optimal 
performance level. We showed that aligning technical skills with pacing requirements of 
specific race sections, by balancing stroke smoothness and speed production while better 
preserving initial SL, seems to be a discriminant kinematic characteristic of optimal 
performers. Then, swimmers tend to save energy with an economical style in the first half of 
the 5-km, and switch to a speed-oriented style that reduces mechanical proficiency thereafter.

Accepted author manuscript version reprinted, by permission, from International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2024- 0305 ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT / CLEAN COPY Abstract Purpose: To investigate technical regulation mechanisms of long-distance swimmers that differentiate optimal pacing strategies and the underlying kinematic parameters. Methods: Twenty-one national and international swimmers equipped with a sacrum-worn IMU performed during 5000m indoor French championships. Percentage of critical swimming speed (CSS), stroke rate (SR), stroke length (SL), jerk cost (JC), stroke index (SI), and mechanical proficiency score (MPS) were computed by lap. Athletes were divided into groups of pacing effectiveness based on optimal potential performance level (OPPL) -optimal (nearOPPL) and suboptimal (farOPPL)- using functional clustering of %CSS. Race sections were analyzed with a change-in-slope detection method. Common stroke regulation abilities and deviations by pacing groups were profiled by fitting hierarchical generalized additive models between mechanical variables and laps. Results: The two clusters were discriminated by %CSS sustainment (p<0.01). Optimal performers showed a +41.4% more stable pacing (2 race sections vs. 3 for farOPPL) and a +36.7% higher end-spurt, with a trend combining higher overall SR (p=0.08) with lower JC (p=0.17). Functional profiles showed that maintaining a higher SL and SI in a fatigued state, rather than overall values, allows to reach OPPL (p<0.001). High regulation of MPS across the race, in line with pacing expectations of particular race sections, is a game-changer to sustain CSS (p<0.001). Conclusions: Specific profiles of stroke regulations, regarding tradeoff between stroke smoothness and resultant speed, lead to optimal pacing during 5000m. The results of this study enhances the technical understanding of an optimal pacing in long-distance pool races for coaches and swimmers.
